You start every Claude chat from zero.

Every time, you explain who you are, what you do and how you like answers.

Engineers at Google and Cloudflare don't. They keep a file of instructions their AI reads first, and a post listing theirs got 4,800 bookmarks this week.

You don't need GitHub for this. Claude and ChatGPT both have a box for it:
→ Claude: Settings → personal preferences. For one project: project instructions.
→ ChatGPT: Settings → Personalization → Custom instructions.

What good rules look like:
→ Answer in under 150 words unless I ask for more.
→ Plain words. No jargon, no "great question".
→ If my request is unclear, ask one question before answering.
→ Never invent numbers, quotes or sources.

Prompt 1: The interview (builds your file)

"Interview me to write my personal AI instructions. Ask one question at a time, 12 questions max: my role and what I work on, who I write for, the tone I like and hate, formats I want (length, bullets or prose, tables), habits that annoy me in AI answers, what to do when my request is unclear, and what I never want it to do. Then write my instructions as short Do and Don't rules, under 200 words, in one block I can copy. Finally, list 3 things I should add later."

Prompt 2: The project file

"I'm starting a project: [describe]. Write project instructions an AI will read before every chat: the goal, the audience, key facts and numbers, decisions already made, style rules, and what 'done' looks like. Under 250 words. Flag anything you had to guess with [?]."

Prompt 3: The weekly fix

"Here are my current instructions: [paste]. Here's what annoyed me in AI answers this week: [list]. Rewrite the instructions to fix it. Keep them under 200 words and tell me what you changed."

Test it: ask the same question in a new chat before and after. If the answer didn't change, your rules are too vague. Rewrite them as orders.

Our take: 20 minutes on this file saves you the same 3 paragraphs in every chat for the rest of the year.

You can put an AI teammate in your Slack today. 53 million people watched the launch. Most teams will give it zero instructions and quietly switch it off within a week.

Grok Bot 1.0 came out of beta yesterday. Bots are shared across a team, live in Slack and Teams, join your calls, offer to pick up work before you ask, and learn from everyone who works with them. Team Bots are on the Team and Enterprise plans.

Here's what the launch thread skips. A bot with no job description is Clippy with calendar access. You would never hire a person and say "help out". You tell them what they own.

The same brief works in Grok Bot, a Claude Project or a custom GPT, so you can run it on whatever you already pay for.

Prompt: Teammate brief
"You are joining our team as [role, e.g. support lead for our SaaS]. You own one outcome: [outcome, e.g. every customer email answered within 4 hours]. Do these without asking: [3 tasks]. Always ask before: [3 actions, e.g. refunds, anything sent to a customer, deleting data]. Your context lives in [tools or docs]. Every Friday post a 5-line report: what you closed, what is stuck, what you need from me, one thing you would change, one risk you see. If you cannot finish something, say so in the channel instead of guessing. Before your first task, ask me the 6 questions that would most change how you do this job, then wait for my answers."

Run it once. The bot that asks six good questions first is the one your team is still using in March.

Most agent failures are hiring failures. Nobody wrote the job.
